name: Lump of labour fallacy
aliases: Theory of the Lump of Labour
statement: The claim names a belief that a fixed quantity of work exists, so that a person who works more, or a worker who arrives, must take employment from someone else.
meaning: Two separate claims travel under this name and the entry keeps them apart. The first is psychological: that ordinary people hold a fixed-work belief and reason from it to policy. The second is economic: that hours cuts, later retirement, immigration and automation do not move employment one for one, so the belief is wrong. Neither claim settles the other. Schloss, who named the theory, described it as the view that there is a certain fixed amount of work to be done, and that each worker should take care not to do too much, so that the Lump of Labour may be spread out thin over the whole body of work-people. That wording is identical in his 1891 article and in the 1894 book chapter. His target was restriction of output by workers on piece-wage, and his analogy was the popular objection to machinery. Daniel Kinderman, quoted by Walker, notes that the fixed amount can mean two different things, a ceiling on labour demand or an assumption that labour demand does not respond to labour cost, and the two carry different arguments. This collection covers the general part-to-whole error at entry 450 and the wider fixed-pie belief at entry 105. The lump of labour is narrower than either. It is a claim about one market, and it is usually deployed against a named policy rather than as a description of reasoning.

origin.note: Walker traces the earliest known reference to a fallacious theory of the lump of labour to Schloss's article 'Why Working-Men Dislike Piece-Work'. Walker gives its pages as 1(3), 312 to 326, and Wels and Macnicol give 311 to 326. The article was read here from the Internet Archive scan of volume I. Its index entry, its opening page and its closing page all give 311 to 326, so Walker is out by one page at the start. Chapter V of the second edition of Schloss's book repeats the passage at pages 43 to 47. The argument that shorter hours rest on a fixed-work belief was made three years later by John Rae, in Eight Hours for Work. Walker records that Rae favoured the eight-hour day, denied it would relieve unemployment, and wrote that reducing hours to create jobs was not a simple sum in arithmetic. Charles Beardsley answered him in the Quarterly Journal of Economics in 1895, arguing that Rae relied on the wages-fund doctrine he attributed to others. Walker records that a 1901 London Times series and a 1904 National Association of Manufacturers pamphlet turned the phrase against the eight-hour day itself.

evidence: The psychological claim has been measured by survey. Achim Kemmerling used Eurobarometer data on agreement that people in their late 50s should give up work to make way for the young and unemployed, and reports about a quarter agreeing in the United Kingdom against more than 90% in Greece. Those two country figures are read from his own summary of the article rather than from the article, which is closed access and was not obtained. His abstract states that voters in some European countries do not think an employment trade-off between older and younger workers exists while in others it is the dominant view, and that the belief tracks policy preferences on early retirement. Special Eurobarometer 469, on the integration of immigrants, put a flat statement to respondents. 39% agreed that immigrants take jobs away from workers in their country and 57% disagreed, against 72% who agreed that immigrants make it easier to fill jobs for which it is hard to find workers. Bryan Caplan measured the gap between the public and economists on related items in the Survey of Americans and Economists on the Economy. Ordered logits on an economist dummy give a coefficient of -2.77, z = -17.50, for whether technology displacing workers is a reason the economy is not doing better, and -2.72, z = -18.54, for company downsizing. On the twenty-year outlook for new technology, foreign competition and downsizing, economists averaged 1.92 on a scale where 2 is good, and Caplan writes that the public remained neutral. The economic claim has been tested against particular episodes and the results do not point one way. Simonetta Longhi, Peter Nijkamp and Jacques Poot pooled 165 estimates from nine studies of regional labour markets and found an unweighted mean elasticity of native employment to immigration of -0.024, meaning a 1% rise in immigration lowers local native employment by 0.024%. The mean was -0.005 on United States data and -0.032 on European and Israeli data. They read their own result as settling the question, writing that the idea of fixed aggregate employment in a given area can be considered as a fallacy. Jennifer Hunt used 30 German manufacturing industries from 1984 to 1994. Actual hours fell by 0.88 to 1 hour for each one-hour cut in standard hours, and the straight-time hourly wage rose 2% to 2.4%. Her employment estimates are imprecise, and the point estimates indicate that employment of men fell. Bruno Crepon and Francis Kramarz studied the French cut from 40 hours to 39 in February 1982 and found the same sign. Workers on 40 hours or more in March 1981 became less likely to be employed in 1982 than comparable workers on 36 to 39 hours, with estimated effects between 2.6% and 3.9%, and a lower bound of 4.1% in their second design. Their table 4 gives one-year employment losses in 1982 of 8.2% for workers on 40 hours against 6.6% for those on 39, and two-year cumulated losses of 16.5% against 12.6%.

replication.headline: The belief is found wherever it is looked for, and the economic proposition the fallacy label asserts comes out differently across immigration, hours and retirement.
replication.detail: On the psychological side the results agree. Eurobarometer 469 puts agreement that immigrants take jobs away at 39% across the European Union, Kemmerling's Eurobarometer series puts agreement with an age trade-off at about a quarter in the United Kingdom and over 90% in Greece, and Caplan's lay-expert gaps on technological displacement and downsizing are among the largest in his set. On the economic side the answer depends on which policy is asked about. Immigration is where the fallacy claim does best. Longhi, Nijkamp and Poot's pooled elasticity is -0.024, and the same meta-analysis gives -0.005 for the United States against -0.032 elsewhere. The Mariel boatlift, which raised the Miami labour force by 7%, is the sharpest case. David Card reported virtually no effect on the wages or unemployment rates of less-skilled workers. George Borjas, restricting attention to high school dropouts, reported that their wages fell by 10% to 30%, implying an elasticity between -0.5 and -1.5. Giovanni Peri and Vasil Yasenov applied the synthetic control method to non-Cuban high school dropouts and found no significant wage difference. Michael Clemens and Jennifer Hunt trace the disagreement to a shift in the racial composition of very small Current Population Survey subsamples, specific to Miami and unrelated to the boatlift, and read the refugee-wave evidence as showing small effects on average native workers. Work-sharing runs against the hopes of its advocates rather than against the fallacy claim. Hunt's German study finds employment of men falling when standard hours fell, and Crepon and Kramarz find job losses in France in 1982. Retirement is where the results genuinely disagree. Ignacio Apella's panel of 11 Latin American countries from 2002 to 2019 found a positive correlation between the employment rates of older adults and young people. Marco Bertoni and Giorgio Brunello, evaluating Italy's 2011 pension reform, estimate that for every 1,000 senior workers locked into employment the reform cut youth employment by 273 and prime-age employment by 199. Jacques Wels and John Macnicol's British time-series found employment of the over-65s positively associated with youth unemployment and inactivity in their preferred lagged model, adjusted R-squared 0.37, Durbin-Watson 2.26. On automation, Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo estimate that one more industrial robot per thousand workers reduces the United States employment-to-population ratio by 0.2 percentage points and wages by 0.42%, a displacement effect that is real and far short of one for one.

study.cite: Longhi, S., Nijkamp, P., & Poot, J. (2006). The impact of immigration on the employment of natives in regional labour markets: a meta-analysis. IZA Discussion Paper No. 2044.

limits: The label has a published critic and the criticism is about its use rather than about labour economics. Tom Walker argues in the Review of Social Economy that the authenticity of the fallacy claim is questionable and that explanations of it are inconsistent and contradictory. He counts no fewer than 17 articles in The Economist decrying the supposed fallacy between 1993 and 2005, and lists policy papers for the French Ministry of Finance, the UK Department for Work and Pensions, the OECD and the International Labour Organization that deploy it. His substantive point is that the claim is used in place of an argument. Sydney Chapman's 1909 presidential address on the hours of labour, which Hicks in 1932 called the classical statement of the theory of hours in a free market, holds that shorter hours can raise output through recovery from fatigue. Chapman argues that uncombined employers keep the working day longer than suits even them, from short-sightedness or fear that a rival will reap the gain. Walker writes that Chapman's analysis has never been refuted, only displaced by a simplifying assumption, and that Keynes, Pasinetti and Commons all treated reduced working time as a route to fuller employment without being answered. Wels and Macnicol make the parallel complaint about retirement, that the fallacy is used as an assumption rather than examined, and that Ros Altman's 2015 government report called the idea roundly discredited by academic studies while citing three sources in a few lines. Their own counter-calculation should be read as what it is. Converting British part-time jobs to half a full-time equivalent, they put 1951 at about 21,710,000 full-time equivalents and 2018 at 27,981,000, a rise of 29% against population growth of just over 30%, and conclude that there is a lump of labour. That is an accounting exercise on aggregate stocks, not an estimate of a policy effect, and the 50% conversion factor is their choice. Every economic figure quoted here is an estimate for one episode under one design. Two are quoted at one remove and say so. Acemoglu and Restrepo's published figures were read from the abstract as carried by RePEc and by MIT's Shaping the Future of Work, because the Journal of Political Economy refused the request on 17 August 2026; their 2017 working paper gave a wider range, 0.18 to 0.34 percentage points and 0.25% to 0.5%. Bertoni and Brunello's figures come from the abstract their publisher deposited at Crossref. The psychological figures have the mirror problem. Agreement with a survey statement about immigrants or older workers is not the same act as inferring that total work is capped, and no instrument located here separates the two.
misreadings: The commonest error is about Schloss. He aimed the phrase at workers restricting their output on piece-wage, and the modern use, against policies that shorten hours, comes from Rae rather than from him. Schloss says on page 326 of the 1891 article, and again on page 47 of the book, that with the question of the length of the working-day we have here nothing to do, and adds that a reduction of the hours of labour, say to eight in the day, may readily be admitted to be, on grounds both economic and social, highly desirable. The examples he gives are the Bradford lodge of the Labourers' Union cautioning members against doing double the work, and, in the book only, a Trades Union Magazine passage holding that a man earning 40s by task-work where the day rate is 20s robs his fellow of a week's employment. The second error is to treat the fallacy claim and the empirical claim as one. Showing that a fixed-work belief is common says nothing about whether a given policy displaces workers, and showing that a policy does not displace workers says nothing about why anyone believed it would. Walker's complaint is that the label lets an author skip the second question by winning the first. The third is direction. In several settings the disputed finding runs against the fallacy claim rather than for it, and the arguments are then between economists. Borjas against Card and Peri on Mariel, with Clemens and Hunt arriving later to explain the gap, is a dispute inside the literature rather than between economists and the public. The fourth is that work-sharing results are read as evidence for a lump of labour. They are not. Hunt and Crepon and Kramarz find that cutting hours failed to spread the work, which is the fallacy claim's own prediction. The fifth is scope. Zero-sum thinking at entry 105 is a general belief about social relations with its own scales and its own correlates, and the fallacy of composition at entry 450 is a form of argument. This entry is neither. It is a specific economic proposition about the quantity of work, which is why the evidence for it consists of employment elasticities rather than of judgement tasks. No experiment locating a lump of labour belief in individuals, as distinct from a survey item measuring agreement with one, was found in searches of Crossref, PubMed, OpenAlex and the open web on 17 August 2026.

sources.text: Schloss, D. F. (1891). Why working-men dislike piece-work. The Economic Review, 1(3), 311-326. Full text read from the Internet Archive scan of volume I. Source for the naming of the theory, its definition, the dockyard washer-maker's remark on page 324, the Bradford lodge rule, the steam-plough analogy and the endorsement of the eight-hour day on page 326. The volume index gives the start page as 311. Crossref holds no record for the article, so it carries no identifier.

Schloss, D. F. (1894). Methods of Industrial Remuneration (2nd ed.). London: Williams and Norgate. Full text read from the Internet Archive scan. Chapter V, pages 43 to 47, repeats the naming of the theory of the Lump of Labour, its definition, the dockyard washer-maker's remark, the Bradford lodge rule, the steam-plough analogy and the endorsement of the eight-hour day on page 47, and adds the Trades Union Magazine passage on page 46. The index entry gives pages 38, 38n and 43 to 47.

Walker, T. (2007). Why economists dislike a lump of labor. Review of Social Economy, 65(3), 279-291. Full text read from the PDF at timeworkweb.com. Source for the attribution to Schloss 1891, for Rae, Beardsley, the 1901 Times series and the 1904 manufacturers' pamphlet, for the count of 17 Economist articles between 1993 and 2005, for Kinderman's ceiling-or-floor point, and for the account of Chapman, Hicks, Keynes, Pasinetti and Commons.

Kemmerling, A. (2016). The end of work or work without end? How people's beliefs about labour markets shape retirement politics. Journal of Public Policy, 36(1), 109-138. Crossref confirms author, title, journal, volume, issue, pages and year, and its abstract was read there. The article is closed access. Cambridge Core returned an error on 17 August 2026 and OpenAlex records no open copy in any repository, so it was not obtained. The country figures of about a quarter in the United Kingdom and over 90% in Greece, and the Eurobarometer 2001 series behind them, come from the author's own summary of the article on the LSE European Politics blog.

European Commission (2018). Special Eurobarometer 469: Integration of immigrants in the European Union. Summary read from the Commission PDF; fieldwork was October 2017. It carries the 39% agreeing and 57% disagreeing that immigrants take jobs away from workers, the 72% on hard-to-fill jobs, and the wording of question QA9.

Caplan, B. (2002). Systematically biased beliefs about economics: robust evidence of judgemental anomalies from the Survey of Americans and Economists on the Economy. The Economic Journal, 112(479), 433-458. Full text read from the PDF at George Mason University. Table 3 carries the ordered-logit coefficients and z statistics on the economist dummy, including TECH at -2.77 and DOWNSIZE at -2.72, and the surrounding text carries the 1.92 mean on CHANGE20. The string 'lump' does not occur in the article.

Longhi, S., Nijkamp, P., & Poot, J. (2006). The impact of immigration on the employment of natives in regional labour markets: a meta-analysis. IZA Discussion Paper No. 2044. Full text read from the IZA PDF; the abstract, the text and Table 2 carry the 165 estimates from nine studies, the unweighted mean of -0.024, the -0.005 and -0.032 sub-sample means, and the authors' own reading of the result as a fallacy. A book-chapter version appeared in Migration and Human Capital in 2009 at pages 173 to 194 and was not obtained, so its figures may differ.

Card, D. (1990). The impact of the Mariel boatlift on the Miami labor market. ILR Review, 43(2), 245-257. Abstract read at Crossref; it is the source for the 7% rise in the Miami labour force and for the finding of virtually no effect on wages or unemployment rates of less-skilled workers. Full text not obtained.

Borjas, G. J. (2017). The wage impact of the Marielitos: a reappraisal. ILR Review, 70(5), 1077-1110. Abstract read at Crossref; it is the source for the 60% dropout share, the 10% to 30% wage fall and the elasticity of -0.5 to -1.5. Full text not obtained.

Peri, G., & Yasenov, V. (2019). The labor market effects of a refugee wave: applying the synthetic control method to the Mariel boatlift. Journal of Human Resources, 54(2), 267-309. Crossref confirms journal, volume, issue and pages. The abstract quoted here was read from NBER working paper 21801, revised June 2017; OpenAlex records no open copy of the published article and it was not obtained.

Clemens, M. A., & Hunt, J. (2019). The labor market effects of refugee waves: reconciling conflicting results. ILR Review, 72(4), 818-857. Abstract read at Crossref and checked against the abstract of NBER working paper 23433. Source for the compositional explanation of the Mariel disagreement and for the reading that refugee waves show small effects on average native-born workers.

Hunt, J. (1999). Has work-sharing worked in Germany? The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 114(1), 117-148. Full text of the published article read from a PDF of the journal scan. Source for the 30 manufacturing industries, the 1984 to 1994 window, the 0.88 to 1 hour fall in actual hours, the 2% to 2.4% wage rise and the conclusion that hours cuts came at the price of lower overall employment. Her NBER working paper 5724 of August 1996 analysed 201 industries for 1984 to 1989 and reported employment rising by 0.3% to 0.7%; that analysis is not in the published article.

Crepon, B., & Kramarz, F. (2002). Employed 40 hours or not employed 39: lessons from the 1982 mandatory reduction of the workweek. Journal of Political Economy, 110(6), 1355-1389. Full text read from a PDF of the published article; the introduction carries the 2.6% to 3.9% and 4.1% estimates and Table 4 carries the 8.2, 6.6, 16.5 and 12.6 transition rates.

Wels, J., & Macnicol, J. (2019). Is the 'lump of labour' a self-evident fallacy? The case of Great Britain. In Social Policy Review 31 (pp. 221-242). Bristol: Policy Press. Full text read from the working-paper PDF in the ULB repository, which carries Tables 1 and 2, the adjusted R-squared of 0.37, the Durbin-Watson of 2.26, the full-time-equivalent calculation for 1951 and 2018, the Altman quotation and the Schloss pagination of 311 to 326. Crossref confirms the book chapter's pages.

Apella, I. (2024). The fallacy of the lump of labour theory: evidence for Latin America. International Labour Review, 163(1), 49-71. Abstract read at Crossref; it is the source for the 11 countries, the 2002 to 2019 window, the fixed-effects panel and the positive correlation between older and younger employment rates. OpenAlex lists the Wiley PDF as open, and Wiley returned 403 to four requests on 17 August 2026, so the full text was not obtained.

Bertoni, M., & Brunello, G. (2021). Does a higher retirement age reduce youth employment? Economic Policy, 36(106), 325-372. Abstract read at Crossref; it is the source for the 2011 Italian reform, the difference-in-differences design across local labour markets, and the falls of 273 in youth employment and 199 in prime-age employment for every 1,000 senior workers locked in. Full text not obtained. Their 2017 IZA discussion paper 10733 was read and gives a different design and a different figure, 189 fewer workers aged 16 to 34 per thousand.

Acemoglu, D., & Restrepo, P. (2020). Robots and jobs: evidence from US labor markets. Journal of Political Economy, 128(6), 2188-2244. Crossref confirms journal, volume, issue and pages. The published abstract, read as carried by RePEc and by MIT's Shaping the Future of Work, gives 0.2 percentage points and 0.42%; the publisher's page returned 403 on 17 August 2026. NBER working paper 23285 of March 2017 was read direct and gives 0.18 to 0.34 percentage points and 0.25% to 0.5%.

Chapman, S. J. (1909). Hours of labour. The Economic Journal, 19(75), 353-373. Full text read from the Internet Archive scan of the September 1909 issue. It is his presidential address to the Economic Science and Statistics Section of the British Association for the Advancement of Science, delivered at Winnipeg. Source for the claim that competition between employers keeps the working day longer than suits them, and for the line that agitation for shorter hours will be constantly breaking out anew.
